answer.rationale: The competitor's price cut creates strong pressure toward promotional_pricing, but memory_73 is explicit and directional: promo pricing buys acquisition and revenue at the cost of 30-day retention, and it carries an inherited instruction not to generalize it as a growth strategy. Under a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, a price match would trade the exact metric we are trying to protect, and the churn spike is itself a retention problem. Of the remaining options, only memory_86 and memory_91 have first-hand archived source records recovered this cycle (exp_86: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, retention +3%; exp_91: engagement +11%, activation +6%, retention +1%). exp_86 is the stronger retention and value-delivery signal, and faster time-to-value is the most direct non-price counter to a price-based attack: it raises realized value before the renewal decision. memory_57 (referrals) is attractive and possibly the better play, but it rests on an unverified consolidated summary and, like memory_73, may hide a caveat the summary dropped; it is queued for verification next cycle rather than acted on now. memory_31 and memory_44 are similarly unverified summaries and are not load-bearing here. Scale is standard_experiment, not broad rollout: exp_86 was confirmed under normal conditions, not under an active competitive price shock against a price-sensitive SMB cohort, so its transfer to this context is an assumption, not a finding. Downstream risk flagged: any result from this cycle will be confounded by the competitor announcement and elevated churn, so it must be written back to memory with that context attached and must not be consolidated into a clean causal claim about onboarding. If churn continues to accelerate, escalate for a human pricing decision rather than letting an agent quietly adopt the retention-harming lever under deadline pressure.
